pronunciation.approximation: STEEX — one syllable, acute on the only vowel there is.
pronunciation.note: Greek Στύξ is monosyllabic — and Greek monosyllables carry the acute on their vowel in modern editions (as Πῦρ carries its circumflex, and φῶς its own). The restoration Stýx keeps that acute: the stress of the single syllable, the only mark the name can bear, exactly where the tradition places it.

domains.title: The River of the Oath
domains.subtitle: The Boundary, the Vow, and the Water the Gods Fear
domains.lead: Stýx is the river by which the gods themselves are bound: the underworld stream whose water makes an oath unbreakable even for Olympos, the eldest daughter of the Ocean, and the mother of Force, Rivalry, Power, and Victory.

mythology.lead: Stýx's myths are about the one thing stronger than the gods: the word that cannot be taken back. She is eldest daughter of the Ocean, mother of the powers that prop Zeús' throne, boundary of the dead — and the water that makes even Olympus keep its promises.

myths.title: The Water the Gods Swear By
myths.text: The Iliad's formula runs through the epic: when Zeus wishes to make an oath unanswerable, he swears 'by the earth and the broad heaven above and the down-flowing water of Styx' (Iliad 15.36–38). Hera, buying the cooperation of Sleep, swears by 'the inviolable water of Styx, which is the greatest and most dread oath for the blessed gods', and pledges him one of the Graces in marriage (Iliad 14.271–279). No epic shows the penalty ever collected — the oath exists precisely so that it need never be. Hesiod's Theogony (793–806) sets the penalty for perjury: the god who pours her water in libation and forswears lies breathless for a full year, cut off from the gods' counsils and feasts for nine more, and returns only in the tenth. Even heaven polices itself — and its police is a river.

myths.title: The Mother of the Reign
myths.text: Hesiod's Theogony (383–403) makes her the hinge of Zeus' kingdom. Styx, eldest daughter of Ocean and Tethys, joined herself to the Titan Pallas and bore four children — Zelos (Rivalry), Nike (Victory), Kratos (Power), and Bia (Force). When the war against the Titans began, she was the first of the immortals to bring her children to Zeus' side, remembering how her father Ocean had suffered under the old dispensation — an eldest daughter's memory of the old regime deciding the new. Zeus rewarded her above all: her children were granted to dwell forever beside him, and the oath by Styx was established as the supreme bond of the gods. The king's throne, the poets say, is propped by a river and her brood — rivalry and victory, power and force, the whole grammar of rule, born of the boundary itself.

myths.title: The Stream of the Under
myths.text: Her water is the underworld's own. Homer sends Odysseus across Ocean to the land of the Cimmerians, where 'the streams of the river Ocean flow' beside the gates of the sun (Odyssey 10.508–515), and the later tradition fixed Styx among the rivers of the dead, with Charon ferrying the unburied across her dark flood (Virgil, Aeneid 6.295–330). Hesiod (Theogony 775–806) makes her a tenth part of Ocean's whole flow, falling from a cliff far beneath the earth, where Night and Day pass each other at the threshold. The dead drink nothing from her, but she fences them: Styx is not a place you cross so much as a condition you accept. In the Orphic gold tablets her name is already there, one of the guardians of the boundary between the living and the company below.

myths.title: Nonakris and the Poison Spring
myths.text: The Greeks placed her on earth in Arcadia. Near the forsaken city of Nonakris in the northern Peloponnese, Pausanias reports (8.17.6–18.6), a water called Styx drips from a high cliff — black, cold beyond any other water, said to destroy whatever vessel it touches. Herodotus (6.74) records the Arcadians' claim that the water can be held in no vessel but a horse's hoof, and links it with the strange end of the Spartan king Kleomenes, who died raving in Arcadian exile. Whether poison spring or simply meltwater of terrible cold, the identification made the divine oath locally tangible: an oath sworn 'by Styx' at Nonakris could point downhill at the thing itself. Later geographers repeat the Arcadian notice, and modern travelers have matched the description to the waterfall above the Krathis gorge. It is the rare case where a goddess's material trace outlasted her cult.

lore.syncretism: Rome transliterated rather than translated her: Styx remained Styx in Virgil and Ovid, the river Charon plies in Aeneid 6 and the oath by which Jupiter himself swears. Dante lowered her into the fifth circle of the Inferno, the marsh where the wrathful tear at one another in the mud — the oath-river become the swamp of anger. Her name became the English adjective 'Stygian' for whatever is dark, cold, and absolute, and her children govern the modern vocabulary: zeal, power, victory. Milton keeps 'Tartarus and Styx' among the fallen angels' retreats in Paradise Lost, and every fantasy underworld since has kept her dark water on file.
lore.culturalLegacy: 'Stygian' is her everyday immortality: the word for the unbreakably dark and the absolutely binding. Her children govern the modern vocabulary — force, zeal, power, victory — and her water gave literature its favourite contract: the deal that cannot be exited, from Faust to fantasy fiction, from sworn testimony in a courtroom to the 'Stygian' underworlds of games, novels, and films, where she appears more often than any other classical borrowing. Astronomers keep the name current: a small moon of Pluto, found by the New Horizons mission, is named Styx. Every 'I swear' spoken in earnest is a small draught of her river, drunk in public.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Stýx is the god of the word that costs something. Contracts, vows, marriage promises, courtroom oaths — all of them work because somewhere, at some depth, a culture decided that speech must bind, and her water is that decision made into a river. She asks the question every oath answers: what are you willing to swear on, and what will it cost you to keep?

The Greeks gave the office to a daughter of the Ocean rather than to a judge or a king — as if to say that binding power is older than law, older than Zeus, as old as the waters under the world. Nine days and nine nights, Hesiod says, an anvil would fall before it touched her stream. Trust itself, the myth implies, is the deepest thing in the universe: everything we build rests on promises, and promises rest on something that cannot be bargained with.
lore.archaeology: The Greeks placed her water in Arcadia: the Styx waterfall near Nonakris in the northern Peloponnese — a cliff-plunge so cold it was said to be her true stream, and Pausanias reports the locals' oath by it. The gorge at Aroania (Krathis river) is shown to visitors still as the legendary drop. Homer's and Hesiod's lines are her oldest attestations; the Roman poets from Virgil to Statius keep her darkly flowing in every underworld scene.
